newsitem.title: USA: Ford's U.S. February sales drop 3.2 percent.
newsitem.headline: Ford's U.S. February sales drop 3.2 percent.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Tuesday its U.S. car and light truck sales fell 3.2 percent in February from a record pace a year ago, rounding out a down month for Detroit's Big Three automakers.

Ford's sales of light trucks, including minivans, sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks, rose 1.5 percent from February 1996 to 163,117. But car sales at the nation's No. 2 automaker continued to slump, falling 8.5 percent to 128,945.
Overall light vehicle sales at Ford slid to 292,062 from 314,223 in February 1996.

The percentage changes are based on the average number of vehicles sold per day, instead of the monthly totals, because the number of selling days in a month vary from year to year. February had 24 selling days, one less than a year ago.
On Monday, General Motors Corp. posted light vehicle sales of 352,234, a decline of 7.4 percent for the month, while Chrysler Corp. sales were down 2.8 percent to 193,983.
Bob Rewey, Ford's group vice president of marketing and sales, cautioned that February truck sales were up against year-ago comparisons that rank as the strongest monthly selling rate ever reached.
Rewey blamed weak car sales on the growing popularity of trucks and higher retail incentives from Japanese automakers.

"The yen's weakness has enabled Japanese companies to take very aggressive competitive actions, leading to significant share shifts, especially in the car market, where most of their production capacity is concentrated," Rewey said in a statement.

Sales of Ford division cars fell in nearly every segment, bringing the division's total car sales down by 11.7 percent. Taurus sales finished the month at 26,651, off 8 percent, but still ahead of the 25,440 rival Honda Accords sold in Feburary. The Taurus beat out the Accord last year as the top-selling car in the United States in what has become a hotly contested annual race for the No. 1 spot.
Mercury division car sales rose 2.8 percent, with positive showings by the Grand Marquis, Cougar, Sable and Tracer. Lincoln car sales suffered a 7 percent drop.

Ford's sport utility vehicle sales were held back by short supplies of the Expedition due to a three-week strike by a seat-maker that disrupted prodution. Rewey said the time it takes to retrofit Expeditions with seats will continue to affect March sales of the popular model, one of Ford's most profitable vehicles.

Also on the truck side F-Series sales were down 3.4 percent; Explorer sport utility vehicle sales were off 10.4 percent; Windstar minivan sales fell 0.6 of a percent; sales of the Ranger compact pickup rose 5.4 percent; and Villager minivan sales were unchanged on a percentage basis.
Of the Japanese automakers that had reported by late Tuesday, Mazda Motor Corp.'s U.S. sales toppled 16.4 percent to 15,333. February U.S. sales of Isuzu Motor Co. Ltd. were down 17 percent to 6,531.
Volkswagen of America Inc. sales were up 6.5 percent to 9,249. VW's Audi of America Inc. unit had sales of 2,448, a 31 percent jump that represents its best February sales in 11 years.
